claims.claim: Origen of Alexandria was an early Christian theologian, biblical scholar, and exegete who lived from approximately 185 to 253/254 CE.
Origen was head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria and was later ordained priest by the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem.
The Homilies on Leviticus were delivered in Alexandria during a three-year liturgical cycle between 238 and 244 CE.
Theoctistus gave Origen the responsibility to deliver homilies during the three-year liturgical cycle of the Church in which the Old Testament and Gospel would be fully covered.
The homilies were delivered at non-eucharistic meetings attended by catechumens as well as full members of the Church, and at eucharistic meetings for full members only.
The Homilies on Leviticus were translated into Latin by Rufinus.

Rufinus admitted to having changed the text by condensing the homilies and expanding some of the explanations, and he made more changes to the Homilies on Leviticus than to Origen's homilies on other books of the Pentateuch.
The work survives through Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's original Greek text.

The homilies provide valuable insights on the third-century Church, touching on topics of conversion from sin, works of piety, baptism, Lent and fasting, the ordination of a priest, and the process of Christian discipline.
Origen's most significant theological contribution in these homilies is his doctrine of the Trinity, which influenced the Trinitarian debates of the fourth and fifth centuries.
Origen believed that the meaning of Scripture was threefold—literal, moral, and spiritual—with the spiritual interpretation being the most important.
